findings.title: Findings converge on the run-history record (D2, D3, D4, D9)
findings.why_it_matters: Nine findings land on one mechanism: the sidecar that stores a start and a finish record per run, with a PID, last 20 per kind, written by four kinds of run. The two critics pull it in opposite directions. Senior-engineer's fixes harden the record (an age bound on `running`, a boot id beside the PID, a database identity, a last-N rule). Structural-minimalist's fixes shrink it (no list, no start record, no sync writer, one file). Several answers cancel each other: Finding 9's escalation reads the list that Finding 4 deletes, Finding 10 adds identity to a PID that Finding 3 stops storing, and Finding 2's age comes from a start record that Finding 3 removes. Finding 11 only works if Findings 4 and 5 land. Should this mechanism be re-evaluated as a whole, including whether its failure modes are limitations to accept and document, rather than answered finding by finding?
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the run-history record before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions: Does any catalog row need more than the newest record and the last success? Which of #234's acceptance criteria hold as written, and which should change? Does state that already exists answer any of this? What must happen to the record when the database is replaced? Which failure modes are worth handling, and which are limitations to document?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the run-history record before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions: Does any catalog row need more than the newest record and the last success? Which of #234's acceptance criteria hold as written, and which should change? Does state that already exists answer any of this? What must happen to the record when the database is replaced? Which failure modes are worth handling, and which are limitations to document?

findings.title: A hung or livelocked job reads as "working on it" forever and mutes the stale-backlog alarm
findings.why_it_matters: A start record whose PID is alive is `running` with no age limit (D4). D6 maps a live job to "working on it", and D7 says "A live backfill PID means 'working on it' regardless". A swapping or deadlocked backfill is alive but making no progress. The PID guard then skips every later backfill, findings stay "working on it", and `doctor` exits 0 indefinitely. This is the most expensive failure the tool can see, and it reports it as fine.
findings.recommended: A: Apply D7's live-PID override, and the "Job running now" row, only while the run is younger than `backfill_stale_hours`; past that it is a needs-action "run looks stuck" finding.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Start records in the sidecar duplicate what the PID guard already knows
findings.why_it_matters: D4 builds start records plus a PID probe to tell `running` from `killed`, but D8 puts both in "working on it", and "Job running now" is already a live PID-guard check. The critic's fix, finish records only, removes the second write on every sync and all PID storage. It also has two costs the critic didn't name. It fails two #234 acceptance criteria ("record start, finish" and "A run killed before it can finish is detectable as unfinished"). And `killed` is more than display text: it is the only evidence outside the logs that a run was OOM-killed. A third shape avoids both costs: the existing PID marker is already a start record. It is written at acquire and removed in `finally`, so a killed run leaves a marker with a dead PID, and `live_pid_holder` never reaps it.
findings.recommended: C: Write a finish record only, and derive `running` or `killed` from the existing PID marker: present with a live PID is running, present with a dead PID is killed.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The bounded history is never read as a history
findings.why_it_matters: Every consumer reads one record per kind. D6 and D8 use the newest run, D7 uses the last successful backfill, and D13 uses the newest sync. No finding, flag or output shows a list. The design still builds a 20-per-kind list, an eviction policy and a shared-versus-per-kind comparison, for data read at depth 1 or 2. D3 itself says "current state, not long history, drives findings", and 20 syncs is about two hours.
findings.recommended: A: Replace the list with a fixed per-kind `{last, last_ok}` record.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: "Last sync" can come from the database, removing the per-sync write
findings.why_it_matters: Sync records runs for D13's `last sync 2 min ago` and a sync-failure finding. `import_log.imported_at` is already set on every upsert, by both sync and import, so `SELECT MAX(imported_at) FROM import_log` answers "when did ccrecall last ingest a transcript" with no new state. One critic claim is overstated: generic sync failures do not reach `embedding-status.json`, which sync writes only for a vector-unavailable failure; other exceptions go only to `ccrecall-sync.log`. Dropping the writer entirely would therefore remove the only non-log signal for a failing sync. The Stop-path framing is also softer than stated, because sync runs in a detached process and not on the hook thread. The gain is less state, not hook latency.
findings.recommended: C: Record sync only on failure; `last sync` becomes `last ingested` from `import_log`.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A sidecar that outlives a deleted database vouches for the fresh one
findings.why_it_matters: D2 accepts that "a stale file can remain after deleting only the DB" as if it were cosmetic. After a delete and re-import, the old file still says "backfill ok 2h ago", so D7's first clause is false and a full queue of never-embedded sessions does not become needs action until the old timestamp passes the limit. A stale "failed" record can also raise a finding about a database it never touched. `unrepairable.json` is protected by fingerprints; run history has no equivalent. The damage is bounded: the verdict is "working on it" with a large count, not "healthy", `status` shows a low embedded percentage, and the clock escalates within `backfill_stale_hours`. But the fix line is missing at the moment a user is recovering.
findings.recommended: B: Store the database inode in the sidecar and treat a mismatch as empty history.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: D11's Recommendation contradicts its Ratified line
findings.why_it_matters: D11's Recommendation keeps today's JSON fields, hides `--check-ingestion`, keeps `--days` and titles the PR `feat:`. Its Ratified line replaces the JSON, removes both flags and titles the PR `feat!:` with a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer. The Deciding factor and Pick lines also argue the old option. A builder who reads the Recommendation first ships an unmarked break, or the wrong contract, in a public package's `--json`.
findings.chosen: Rewrite D11's Deciding factor, Recommendation and Pick lines to state the ratified choice: option C, one reporting shape, `--days` and `--check-ingestion` removed, `feat!:` with one `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer. Pick lines cover A and B. The table's columns already include C, so they stay. The user has already chosen this outcome, so the Ratified sentence's text stays as written.

findings.title: `health.py` already holds a catalog for five of the same conditions
findings.why_it_matters: `_ALERT_PROSE` already defines what five D6 conditions mean, with prose and remedies: can't persist, embeddings failing, tool content incomplete, draft-quality vectors, schema ahead. The design calls `findings.py` "the only place that decides what a state means" and then writes the same conditions again with new text, so a user can be told two different fixes for one condition on the same day. The critic's direction won't work as written: `_ALERT_PROSE` can't import from `findings.py`, because `findings.py` imports `db_vec` and `health.py` is guarded against the vector stack (invariant 3). Ownership has to run the other way. The literal overlap is small: two exact commands and some cause text, since most alert actions are prose.
findings.recommended: A: Put the shared fix commands in constants in `health.py`, import them from `findings.py`, and reword line 26 to say `findings.py` decides for `doctor` and `status`.
findings.chosen: A: Put the shared fix commands in constants in `health.py`, import them from `findings.py`, and reword line 26 to say `findings.py` decides for `doctor` and `status`.

findings.title: A repeatedly OOM-killed run stays filed under "working on it"
findings.why_it_matters: D8 calls `killed` "working on it" because a retry will fix it. A run the OOM killer takes every night stays `killed`, with no count, and each start replaces the last. D7 does escalate, because a killed backfill isn't a success, but only after the limit, and the fix it shows is the command that keeps dying. Nothing tells the user why. Each branch commits on its own, so killed runs still make progress, which softens this.
findings.recommended: B: Keep D8's grouping and have D7's backlog finding name the last backfill's outcome and time.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A reused PID can show a dead run as running
findings.why_it_matters: D4 accepts that a reused PID reads a dead run as `running`, saying it "clears by itself". On a kind with no timer, no next run may come, so that part of D4 is weaker than stated. `kill(pid, 0)` also treats `PermissionError` as alive, so another user's process counts. The critic's "common case" is overstated, though: a false `running` needs a live process to hold that exact PID at the moment of the check.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a reused PID can show a dead run as running until that kind's next run.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Two sidecars where one file could serve
findings.why_it_matters: D9 rejects folding unrepairable ids into the run file because it would be rewritten on every sync and grow with the problem. If Findings 4 and 5 land, the rewrite objection goes away, leaving one extra file, lock path and test fixture per database. The critics disagree: senior-engineer says "the fingerprint design is sound; I do not recommend revisiting D9". The critic's claim that the ids are a negative cache the design forbids doesn't hold: D9 keeps repair's retries unchanged, and only `doctor` reads the file.
findings.recommended: B: Keep `<db>.unrepairable.json` as its own file.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: D10 calls `status` safe in prompts, but D1 makes it take 6 to 19 seconds
findings.why_it_matters: D10's table and Ratified line call `status` safe "in a prompt or `set -e` script" and "a glance safe in prompts and chains". That's true of its exit code and false of its time: D1 ratified about 5.7s warm and an estimated 19s cold. Posture says `status` "should feel like a glance". The critic's other concern doesn't hold as a design problem: `_readonly_connection` opens no transaction and nothing sets `isolation_level`, so each `SELECT` holds its own snapshot, and the classification's per-session queries finish with `fetchall`. No snapshot is pinned across the classify step, and WAL readers don't block writers.
findings.recommended: A: Reword D10 and Posture: safe by exit code, and not fast enough for a shell prompt.
findings.chosen: A: Reword D10 and Posture: safe by exit code, and not fast enough for a shell prompt.

findings.title: Three modules for one pipeline
findings.why_it_matters: `findings.py` computes, `doctor.py` renders in full, and `status.py` renders two lines, with an identical `--json` shape (D11). After D11 removes `collect_status` and `print_status_report`, `status.py` is left holding `run` and helpers. Line 314 also says both commands use `status._readonly_connection`, so `doctor.py` and possibly `findings.py` import from `status.py` while `status.py` imports from `findings.py`, a cycle unless the connection helper moves. The critic ranks this low: "Not important enough to defend if the author prefers separation."
findings.recommended: A: Keep `findings.py` and put both renderers, the shared JSON shape and both `run` functions in one module.
findings.chosen: A: Keep `findings.py` and put both renderers, the shared JSON shape and both `run` functions in one module.

findings.title: History is per database, but PID guards and embedding status are global
findings.why_it_matters: D2 separates history by database, but the other state `doctor` reads isn't separated. PID markers and `embedding-status.json` live in `RUNTIME_DIR`. `doctor --db copy.db` therefore reports "Job running now" for the live install's import and "embedding unavailable" from the live sidecar, inferring one database's state from another's evidence. #234's criterion concerns the history, which stays correct.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: with `--db`, job and embedding findings describe the whole install, not that database.
findings.chosen: C: Accept as a known limitation: with `--db`, job and embedding findings describe the whole install, not that database.

findings.title: `flock` on the write path blocks with no timeout
findings.why_it_matters: "Best-effort, can never fail a run" covers exceptions but not `fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX)`, which has no timeout. A stuck holder or a slow rename stalls the run while it holds its PID guard, and a kill between `mkstemp` and `replace` leaves a `*.tmp` beside the database. Separately, `logging.md` requires an `except` that swallows an error to log it, so recording failures need a log line rather than the bare `contextlib.suppress` used around today's sidecar writes; that applies whichever option is chosen.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a stopped lock holder or hung filesystem can stall a run's recording.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Bad sidecar content has no stated handling
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: multi-user machine, not the stated solo case. D4 and D8 consume the file with no stated validation. An entry with a PID of 0, a negative PID, a non-dict, or a `finished_at` earlier than `started_at` can mislead a check. A check that raises is already covered by Posture's per-check isolation, and the `health.py` tolerant reader is the existing convention, so what is actually open is field-level validation and an explicit finding. The critic's "truncated write after a crash" trigger doesn't apply: `atomic_write_json` replaces the file in one step.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a hand-edited sidecar can mislead a finding until the next run rewrites it.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a hand-edited sidecar can mislead a finding until the next run rewrites it.

findings.title: `backfill_stale_hours` adds a contract for few installs
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a public package with many differently scheduled installs. The only second case the design names is the maintainer's nightly install at 36h. A setting becomes a contract once released, by D7's own text. The critic also raises the two-clock rule, though D7's table shows that rule avoids a false alarm after downtime. The critic flags this as already ratified and raises it once.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: one more documented setting, used by few installs.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: one more documented setting, used by few installs.

findings.title: `status` and `doctor` can read the sidecar and the database at different instants
findings.why_it_matters: Run history and the database have no common snapshot. A sync that has committed but not yet written its finish record reads as `running` beside a database already showing the new state, and the reverse can also occur. The result is a brief contradictory finding. It is cosmetic, but D1's "no staleness to explain" holds only for database facts. The two sides: precise wording in the design against no change for a seconds-long, self-clearing oddity.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a run finishing during a read can show a brief contradictory finding.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a run finishing during a read can show a brief contradictory finding.

findings.title: Findings converge on reading run state from PID markers
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger's decision on killed-run detection (D4) reads `running`, `killed` and `stuck` from the PID marker each job already has. Five findings land on that one signal from different sides. A live PID may not be ccrecall (Finding 2). A dead PID may not be a run that ever started (Finding 7). A hung sync is left out of the marker checks (Finding 8). A dead marker can sit beside a newer finish record (Finding 9). An empty marker is neither live nor dead (Finding 10). All of them come from a marker holding a bare PID, written by whichever process acquired it, sometimes the parent. A marker or job-written entry that said more than a bare PID would remove at least the local fixes for Findings 7 and 10. Should the mechanism be re-evaluated, or are these rare cases to patch or accept one at a time?
findings.recommended: B: Keep PID markers as D4 chose and resolve the five findings individually.
findings.chosen: B: Keep PID markers as D4 chose and resolve the five findings individually.

findings.title: `<kind>-stuck` tells the user to kill a PID that may belong to another process
findings.why_it_matters: The killed-run decision (D4) accepted that a reused PID shows a dead run as running. It did not weigh what the catalog (D6) does next: past the age limit the finding becomes `<kind>-stuck`, with the fix "kill that PID and rerun". The `fix` field is printed and returned in `--json` as the thing to run, so a person or an agent can kill an unrelated process. The probe only sends signal 0 and counts `PermissionError` as alive, so even a root-owned process reads as a live ccrecall run.
findings.recommended: B: Confirm the PID's command line contains `ccrecall` before reporting `running` or `stuck`, and read a mismatch as `killed`. Also correct D4's sentence, and decide what the guard does about the same mismatch.
findings.chosen: B: Confirm the PID's command line contains `ccrecall` before reporting `running` or `stuck`, and read a mismatch as `killed`. Also correct D4's sentence, and decide what the guard does about the same mismatch.
findings.choice_reason: i think it'd be better to check the pid ourselves, does that require any elevated privileges or anything? and can any package or stdlib module do the branching for linux/mac for us?

findings.title: Interrupted and aborted runs have no defined finish record
findings.why_it_matters: Killed-run detection (D4) only sees processes that skip `finally`. Ctrl-C raises `KeyboardInterrupt`, which runs `finally` and removes the marker. The outcome list (D8) has no interrupted case, so the result depends on what the builder happens to write: a false `backfill-failed` that lasts until the next success, or nothing at all.
findings.recommended: A: A `KeyboardInterrupt` records nothing and removes the marker. State in D8 that `Exception` paths record `failed`, `SystemExit` is not an interruption, and each abort path passes its reason to the recording point. Correct the Assumed bullet.
findings.chosen: A: A `KeyboardInterrupt` records nothing and removes the marker. State in D8 that `Exception` paths record `failed`, `SystemExit` is not an interruption, and each abort path passes its reason to the recording point. Correct the Assumed bullet.

findings.title: A scoped backfill resets the backlog alarm for the whole backlog
findings.why_it_matters: The stuck-queue rule (D7) treats `last_ok` as evidence that the backlog is being worked. `ccrecall backfill embeddings --limit 1` or `--days 14` finishes `ok` after touching a sliver, and the record stores no scope, so it restarts the alarm clock. A scheduled `--days 14` job is the worst case: it never touches older sessions, yet `last_ok` advances every night. The alarm never fires, and `embedding-backlog` says "working on it" indefinitely about work no run will do.
findings.recommended: A: A run with `--limit` or `--days` writes `last` but never advances `last_ok`. State it in D7.
findings.chosen: A: A run with `--limit` or `--days` writes `last` but never advances `last_ok`. State it in D7.

findings.title: A `killed` run is dated by when it started, but reads as when it died
findings.why_it_matters: D4 dates a killed run by the marker's modified time, and D7 plans to print "last run killed at 01:15". The marker is written at acquire, or at spawn for a hook-started job, and is not touched again. A child that finds its own PID doesn't rewrite it. So that time is the start, up to a whole run earlier than the kill (2.45h measured). The finding would state a time the kill didn't happen.
findings.chosen: In D4, say the marker's modified time is when the run started, and that findings state "started at" rather than a kill time. In D7, change the example to "last run, started 01:15, was killed".

findings.title: `doctor`'s database checks don't share a snapshot
findings.why_it_matters: D1's Ratified sentence accepts skew between run history and the database, not between database checks. `_readonly_connection` opens no transaction, so each check reads the database as of its own moment. A sync commit landing during a multi-second scan can count a session as queued in one check and embedded in another, so `embedded_pct` and the `embedding-backlog` split can add up to different totals within one report. A probe confirms it: without a transaction, a read sees a writer's commit straight away. After `BEGIN` on a `mode=ro` WAL connection, the read stays on its snapshot and the writer isn't blocked.
findings.chosen: In D1's recommendation, add: all database checks in one `doctor` or `status` run share one deferred read transaction, opened after the read-only connection and closed at the end. Checks must not commit on it. Transcript files aren't covered, and the cost is that a checkpoint can't pass that snapshot during the scan.

findings.title: A child that dies at startup reads as a killed run that never ages out
findings.why_it_matters: `_spawn_background` writes the child's PID into the marker before the child runs any of its own code. A child that dies first leaves a dead PID, no log and no record, and the design reports `import-killed` as "working on it". Each SessionStart reaps and respawns, so the marker stays young, the age-out in the failed-runs decision (D8) never applies, and a crash loop stays "working on it" indefinitely.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a job that dies before reaching its own code reads as `killed`, and a repeating one stays "working on it" while its harm shows through `fixable-sessions`.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a job that dies before reaching its own code reads as `killed`, and a repeating one stays "working on it" while its harm shows through `fixable-sessions`.

findings.title: A hung sync is named by no finding
findings.why_it_matters: The finding catalog (D6) leaves sync out of running and stuck checks, since a sync is over in seconds. While a hung sync holds its marker, every later Stop skips and records nothing, so syncing stops with no finding that names the cause.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a hung sync isn't named, and its effect shows as `fixable-sessions` once the 15-minute stale-tail window passes.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a hung sync isn't named, and its effect shows as `fixable-sessions` once the 15-minute stale-tail window passes.

findings.title: A dead marker can sit beside a newer finish record
findings.why_it_matters: A finish record is written before the marker is removed; for backfill, the CLI's `finally` removes it after `run()` returns. A kill in that gap leaves a finished run's record next to a dead marker, and D6 then reports `<kind>-killed` for a run that finished. Nothing compares the two.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a kill between the finish record and the marker's removal reads as `killed` until that kind's next run.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a kill between the finish record and the marker's removal reads as `killed` until that kind's next run.

findings.title: An empty or corrupt marker has no defined reading
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: interactive use where `doctor` can run at any moment relative to a spawn. `_spawn_background` creates the marker empty and writes the PID only after `Popen` returns; if `Popen` raises, it stays empty until the next spawn. `live_pid_holder` returns None for missing, corrupt and dead markers alike (probe confirmed), so a reader built on "marker exists and no live holder" reports `import-killed` for a job that's starting. D4 defines only live and dead PIDs. The critics disagree: senior-engineer calls the empty marker harmless because it maps to None, which holds only if the reader treats None as no marker, and then it can't see killed runs either.
findings.recommended: A: Add the reading to D4, and flag it for the builder.
findings.chosen: A: Add the reading to D4, and flag it for the builder.

findings.title: "Unfixable" entries can suppress a session for a reason that isn't the transcript
findings.why_it_matters: The unfixable-sessions decision (D9) says these sessions' transcripts lack the required messages, and `doctor` says retrying won't help. `repair_sessions` counts more than that as unrepairable: any post-repair category other than `ok`, including `pending_tail` (the file grew during repair), and a session with no `project_id`, whose transcript may be fine. Entries key on the source fingerprint alone, while the ok-verdict cache also keys on database coverage. So a database-side fix leaves the entry applying and the message stays wrong. For `missing_source`, `_source_fingerprint` can return None, leaving an entry with nothing to match.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: until the next completed repair, an entry can call a session unfixable because of a file change or a database condition, not a transcript defect.
findings.chosen: C: Accept as a known limitation: until the next completed repair, an entry can call a session unfixable because of a file change or a database condition, not a transcript defect.

findings.title: A persistent `partial` could pin `last_ok`
findings.why_it_matters: The failed-runs decision (D8) marks a backfill `partial` when any branch fails for a retryable reason, such as a lock timeout, and `partial` doesn't advance `last_ok`. A branch that times out on every run would keep the clock from advancing, so D7 could show needs-action with a fix that can't clear it. D8 solved this same trap for content errors only.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a branch that times out on every run keeps `last_ok` from advancing, so the backlog alarm stays up until that writer clears.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a branch that times out on every run keeps `last_ok` from advancing, so the backlog alarm stays up until that writer clears.

findings.title: The run-history read-modify-write contract is only named
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a solo-developer open-source tool where concurrent finishes are routine (sync Stop plus import plus backfill). The storage decision (D2) cites `health.py`'s flock pattern, but `_locked_status_file` only yields a lock, so a caller can read outside it. For `{last, last_ok}` per kind in one file, a read outside the lock can overwrite another kind's fresh record. A failed parse that yields `{}` makes the next writer drop every other kind, including backfill's `last_ok`, and D7 then shows a false alarm. `read_embedding_status` shows that shape: it returns None on any parse error. Separately, `atomic_write_json` removes its temp file only on `Exception`, so a SIGKILL leaves a `.tmp` file beside the database.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an unparseable `<db>.runs.json` is rewritten with only the current kind, so other kinds read as never-run until their next run. Flag for the builder: read inside the lock, as `clear_embedding_failure` does.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: an unparseable `<db>.runs.json` is rewritten with only the current kind, so other kinds read as never-run until their next run. Flag for the builder: read inside the lock, as `clear_embedding_failure` does.

findings.title: A failed sync is cleared by an unrelated session's success
Findings converge on the PID marker as the only evidence of what a live job is and what it is doing
findings.why_it_matters: The PID marker holds a bare PID. Every consumer infers the rest. `read_marker_holder` decides who the holder is by matching a regex against `ps` output (Findings 6, 13). `read_marker` reads the file again to recover the PID it already read (Finding 14). `_spawn_background` treats a marker it can't read as a live holder (Finding 12). `fixable-sessions` and `embedding-backlog` decide what the holder is doing ("the running import repairs them") when the marker can't say whether it is a `--repair-gaps` run or a scoped backfill (Finding 4). Each finding proposes its own local patch: a `ps` flag, a narrower regex, a single read, a reaping rule, a softer message. Should the marker mechanism be re-evaluated instead of patched five times? That includes whether this much inference from a PID is needed at all, and whether the rare failure modes are better accepted and documented.
findings.recommended: B: Keep the marker mechanism as D4 ratified it and resolve Findings 4, 6, 12, 13 and 14 individually.
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the PID marker before addressing Findings 4, 6, 12, 13 and 14 individually. Open questions the re-evaluation must answer: should consumers keep inferring the holder's identity and scope, or should the marker state them? Is the `ps` identity check still needed under whatever answer that gives? Which marker-inferred findings ("running", "working on it", "killed") are worth their failure modes, and which are limitations to document?
findings.choice_reason: we should re-evaluate the pid marker, it was already challenged with 4 findings originally and now 5 more times here.

findings.title: `embedding-unavailable` infers "model not downloaded" from a directory under the doctor process's own environment
findings.why_it_matters: `embedding-unavailable` is a needs-action finding, so it makes `doctor` exit 1. One of its causes is `not is_model_cached_on_disk()`. That check only tests whether `<cache_root>/models--…` exists, where `cache_root` is `$FASTEMBED_CACHE_PATH` or `tempfile.gettempdir()/fastembed_cache` in the process running doctor. Background jobs can run with a different environment. In that case doctor says "isn't downloaded" while search embeds fine, and the fix (`ccrecall-warm-model`) downloads into doctor's directory, not the jobs'. On distros where `/tmp` is tmpfs, the model really is gone after every reboot until the next SessionStart's warm-model finishes. Doctor calls that window needs-action even though a job that fixes it starts automatically.
findings.recommended: A: Keep the cause and its group, and have the message name the path it checked ("not found at <path>"), so a mismatch is visible to the reader.
findings.chosen: A: Keep the cause and its group, and have the message name the path it checked ("not found at <path>"), so a mismatch is visible to the reader.

findings.title: `summary.sessions` is 0 when the count is unknown, in a public JSON field
findings.why_it_matters: `diagnose` initializes `summary = {"sessions": 0, ...}` and overwrites it only when the "session count" check runs, which is the last database check. The `schema-behind` early return and a failed count check both leave the 0 in place on a database that has data. `status` then prints "0 sessions" and `--json` emits `"sessions": 0`, which looks the same as an empty install. `embedded_pct` and `last_sync` already use `null` for unknown, and `summary_line`'s docstring promises to leave out what isn't known. D13 and the Posture make the summary keys a public contract, so the type should be settled before release.
findings.chosen: Initialize `sessions` to `None` (the `no-database` path may keep 0, since no database means none stored). In `summary_line`, omit the sessions part when it is `None`, as already done for `embedded_pct` and `last_sync`. Add a `status` test for the `schema-behind` case.

findings.title: `fixable-sessions` and `embedding-backlog` claim the running job will clear them when the marker can't say what that job does
findings.why_it_matters: When any import marker is live, `fixable-sessions` moves to "working on it", drops its fix, and says "the running import repairs them". Only `import --repair-gaps` repairs. A plain `ccrecall import` or `import --project X` holds the same `PID_KEY_IMPORT` and repairs nothing. In the same way, any live backfill marker turns `embedding-backlog` into "The running backfill is working through them", including a `--limit 1` or `--days 1` run that touches a sliver. The user is told to wait for work that isn't coming, and the command that would do it is withheld. D9's premise is that every fix line stays true, and this one is silently removed.
findings.recommended: A: Keep GROUP_WORKING when a marker is live (as D6 ratified), but change the messages to what is known ("an import is running; it repairs these only if started with --repair-gaps" / "a backfill is running") and keep the fix line visible.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The backlog's "working on it" branch ignores D7's age limit, contradicting its own docstring
findings.why_it_matters: D7 Ratified says "A live run counts as working on it only under the same limit". `backlog_finding`'s docstring says "past the limit, `backfill-stuck` reports that run instead". The code checks only `backfill_marker.running`, never its age. Past `backfill_stale_hours` the report shows `backfill-stuck` (needs action) and, beside it, `embedding-backlog` in "working on it", saying "The running backfill is working through them" with no fix. `fixable-sessions` has the same contradiction against `import-stuck`. The verdict is still needs-attention because of the stuck finding, but the two findings disagree, and the code doesn't do what the ratified rule and its own docstring say.
findings.chosen: In `backlog_finding` and `ingestion_findings`, count a live marker as "working" only when `(scan.now - marker.started_at)` is under `scan.stale_seconds`, so a stuck run falls through to the normal overdue and actionable path, as D7 states. Add one test per finding with a live marker older than the limit.

findings.title: `ps` output width isn't forced, so a clipped command line can reap a live holder
findings.why_it_matters: `is_ccrecall_process` runs `ps -p PID -o command=` and treats any output that succeeds as an identification. If the line is clipped before the `ccrecall` token, it returns False. `read_marker_holder` then raises `ProcessLookupError` and `try_acquire_pid_file` reaps a live marker, so a second embedding backfill can start: the doubled ~8 GB onnxruntime peak the guard exists to prevent. D4 covers `ps` failing or printing nothing, not printing a truncated line. Verified here: procps-ng 4.0.4 with stdout piped prints the full 391-character line by default, but clips to 80 when `COLUMNS=80` is in the environment. A uv-tool install's line (`…/uv/tools/ccrecall/bin/python /home/<user>/.local/bin/ccrecall backfill embeddings`) is over 80 characters, with the token at the end. `ps -ww` printed the full line under `COLUMNS=80`. The senior engineer's claim that macOS clips is unverified. BSD ps(1) documents unlimited width when output isn't a terminal.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A run's outcome defaults to `ok`, so any path that doesn't opt in records success
findings.why_it_matters: `RunRecorder.outcome` starts as `OUTCOME_OK`, and `record_run` writes it on a normal return and on `SystemExit`. Every abort path must call `finish(...)` to avoid recording success, and a forgotten one advances `last_ok`, which gates D7's backlog alarm and `last_sync`. The class docstring says "The run sets its outcome before it returns", which the default contradicts. Gaps that exist today: `import --project X` with a missing or unsafe directory prints an error and records `ok`. A scoped `--project` import advances import's `last_ok`, while backfill passes `advances_ok=not scoped`. Both are latent, because nothing reads import's `last_ok` yet.
findings.recommended: A: Default `outcome` to `None`. Each recorded body calls `recorder.finish(OUTCOME_OK)` on success, and `record_run` records `failed` (reason `error`) when it exits with the outcome still unset.
findings.chosen: A: Default `outcome` to `None`. Each recorded body calls `recorder.finish(OUTCOME_OK)` on success, and `record_run` records `failed` (reason `error`) when it exits with the outcome still unset.

findings.title: `backfill-failed` offers a rerun of the command that just failed when the cause was sqlite-vec
findings.why_it_matters: `run_findings` picks the fix by kind only (`_KIND_FIXES[kind]`). A backfill that failed with `vector_unavailable` yields `backfill-failed` (needs action) with fix `ccrecall backfill embeddings`, the command that just failed. Meanwhile `embedding-unavailable` says to reinstall. The user gets two needs-action findings for one cause, one pointing the wrong way. That breaks D9's "keep every fix line true". (For `model_unavailable`, a rerun can retry the download, so that fix is defensible.)
findings.chosen: In `run_findings`, when `reason == REASON_VECTOR_UNAVAILABLE`, use `REINSTALL_FOR_VEC` as the fix instead of the kind's rerun command. Add a test pinning it.

findings.title: The JSON contract is declared but its values aren't documented, and the README misstates two of them
findings.why_it_matters: D5, D10 and D11 make finding ids, groups, verdict values, summary keys and exit codes a public contract. The README names the fields but not their values. It gives the verdict as "healthy, working on it, or needs attention", while JSON emits `healthy | working | needs-attention` and groups `action | working | none`. It says each finding has "the exact command that fixes it", but `fix` can be prose ("upgrade ccrecall the way you installed it", "report a bug at …", "kill 123, then run …") or null. The id catalog exists only as `FINDING_IDS` in code. Some semantics a caller needs are written nowhere: a finding's group can vary per id, `check-failed` can repeat, `doctor --list` exits 0 whatever the verdict, and with `--json --list <id>` a `sessions` array appears only when that finding is present, so "no finding" and "not listable" look the same.
findings.chosen: Add a short "JSON output" subsection to the README listing the verdict and group enums, the finding-id catalog, that a finding's group can vary while its id is stable, that `fix` may be prose or null, that `check-failed` may repeat, that `sessions` appears only under `--list` on a present listable finding, and the `--list` exit rule. Change "the exact command that fixes it" to "how to fix it".

findings.title: The BREAKING CHANGE footer doesn't list everything that broke
findings.why_it_matters: D11 says the footer names "the removed fields and flags". Commit 1a593dd's footer lists `database`, `schema`, `ingestion`, `tool_content` and `embeddings`. The old `status --json` also returned `db_path`, `db_size_bytes` and `days`, and on a missing database printed `{"error": "database_not_found", ...}`. A script testing `.error` now silently gets null, and nothing in the new output gives the DB path or size. The repo squash-merges, so release-please reads the PR body, and the footer has to be restated there in any case.
findings.chosen: In the PR body's single `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer, also name `db_path`, `db_size_bytes`, `days`, and the `{"error": "database_not_found"}` shape: a missing database now reports a `no-database` finding with verdict `needs-attention`.

findings.title: Contract tests pin less than their names claim
findings.why_it_matters: `test_every_id_a_finding_can_have_is_in_the_catalog` checks four hard-coded ids and never compares emitted ids against `FINDING_IDS`, which is maintained by hand beside literals scattered through findings.py. An id missing from the set makes `doctor --list <id>` a usage error. `"healthy"` and `"working"` are never asserted as JSON literals, so renaming the constants passes the suite. No test writes through `record_run` and reads through `diagnose`, so renaming a `runs.json` key on one side passes both suites. test_import_locking.py asserts `import_project_contained(...) is not None`, which can no longer fail now that it returns a `ProjectFailed` NamedTuple instead of `None`.
findings.chosen: (a) A test that runs `diagnose` across seeded states and asserts every emitted id is in `FINDING_IDS`, plus a literal snapshot of the sorted set. (b) Literal assertions for all three verdict strings in `--json`. (c) One round-trip test: `record_run` followed by `diagnose`. (d) Replace the `is not None` asserts with `not isinstance(..., ProjectFailed)`.

findings.title: `_spawn_background` now treats an unreadable marker as a live holder, permanently
findings.why_it_matters: The new `except PermissionError: return` comes before the reaping handler. `read_marker_holder` already suppresses `PermissionError` from `os.kill`, so a `PermissionError` here can only come from reading the marker file, which says nothing about a holder. A marker owned by another user (for example, created by `sudo -E ccrecall import`) now blocks the import and warm-model spawns on every SessionStart, silently. The manual `ccrecall import --repair-gaps` that `doctor` recommends also skips, because `try_acquire_pid_file` returns False on `PermissionError`, and `doctor`'s `read_marker` returns None for the unreadable marker, so it reports nothing. The only way out is deleting the file by hand. Before this branch, the spawn path reaped on any `OSError`, which healed this. D4 meant to unify the kill-permission case, and that is already handled inside `read_marker_holder`.
findings.recommended: A: Delete the `except PermissionError: return` clause in `_spawn_background`, so an unreadable marker falls into the existing reap-and-retry path, as it did before this branch.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The liveness regex matches any whitespace token, not the executable
findings.why_it_matters: `Audience assumption: a single user whose marker PIDs are reused by a coincidental command, or who launches ccrecall as a module.` `is_ccrecall_process` matches any whitespace token whose basename is `ccrecall` or `ccrecall-<letters>`. When the match is wrong in the false-live direction (`git -C ~/src/ccrecall status`, `rg foo ccrecall` reusing a dead holder's PID), the marker blocks that kind and the stuck fix says to kill an unrelated PID. When it is wrong in the false-dead direction (`python -m ccrecall.cli`, `python -m ccrecall.hooks.sync_current`, or a renamed wrapper), a live marker is reaped and a second backfill can start. Every shipped spawn path uses console scripts, so ordinary users are unaffected.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: only console-script launches are recognized as live holders, and a reused PID whose argv happens to contain a `ccrecall` path reads as live. Note this in the `_CCRECALL_SCRIPT_RE` comment.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: `read_marker` reads the marker three times to build one state
findings.why_it_matters: `Audience assumption: needs a run to reap and re-acquire the marker between two reads microseconds apart.` `read_marker` takes `started_at` from `stat()`. `read_marker_holder` then reads the PID, and on `ProcessLookupError` the handler reads the file again to get the PID for the killed state. If a new run reaps and re-acquires in between, the result is `running=False` with the new, live run's PID and the old run's start time, and doctor says a live process "was killed". The `kill <pid>` text is gated on `running`, so no wrong kill instruction results, only a wrong message for one call.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: in a narrow race, doctor can report a just-started run as killed until the next call.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Losing `runs.json` to a crash or a transient read error turns into a false backlog alarm
findings.why_it_matters: `Audience assumption: single-user local install where power loss or a transient fd/IO error is rare.` `runs.json` is the only source of backfill `last_ok`. `read_json_object` treats every `OSError` (EMFILE, EIO, EACCES) the same as unparseable content and returns `{}`. `write_record` then rewrites a file that was fine with only the current kind. `write_unfixable(replace=False)` drops earlier entries the same way. `atomic_write_json` never fsyncs before the rename, so on filesystems without ext4's rename heuristic a power cut can leave a zero-length file. Either way, backfill `last_ok` is lost, D7's "no successful backfill within the limit" becomes true, and doctor exits 1 until the next unscoped backfill. D2 ratified rewriting an unparseable file but not overwriting a good one after a transient read error.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: losing `runs.json` to a crash or a transient read error can raise a false backlog alarm until the next unscoped backfill.
findings.chosen: C: Accept as a known limitation: losing `runs.json` to a crash or a transient read error can raise a false backlog alarm until the next unscoped backfill.

findings.title: `doctor` run as root can leave root-owned `-wal`/`-shm` files behind
findings.why_it_matters: `Audience assumption: a single-user install where the user runs doctor with elevated rights against their own database.` The Build notes say a `mode=ro` open recreates `-wal` and `-shm` when they're missing. Run as root with the user's database (`sudo -E`, or `--db`), those files are root-owned, and the user's next sync may fail to open the database. A `not-writable` finding invites exactly this kind of sudo diagnosis. Not verified here: whether SQLite removes them on close for a read-only connection.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: running doctor as root against a user's database can leave root-owned WAL files that block that user's next sync.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: running doctor as root against a user's database can leave root-owned WAL files that block that user's next sync.

findings.title: One branch that times out on a lock every run keeps backfill `last_ok` stuck and the backlog alarm up
findings.why_it_matters: The Build call records a backfill as `partial` on any single lock timeout, and only `ok` advances `last_ok`. A nightly backfill that embeds 400 of 401 branches therefore never advances `last_ok`, and doctor says "No full backfill has succeeded … nothing is draining them" while one runs every night. The printed fix (`ccrecall backfill embeddings`) can't clear it while the writer holding that lock is active. The message does say "finished with failures", so it is loud rather than misleading. D8 Ratified already accepts this exact case.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a branch that times out on a lock every run keeps the backlog alarm up until that writer clears (already ratified in D8).
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a branch that times out on a lock every run keeps the backlog alarm up until that writer clears (already ratified in D8).

findings.title: Sync is killed by the 30s hook timeout, so `sync-killed` will be a routine "working on it"
A blocking `flock` with no timeout sits on the Stop-hook path, so a stuck lock kills the hook
The "unfixable" list can mask fixable sessions indefinitely, because repair never re-tests them on a steady-state install
